pages.c07-p02: Describe different types of malware and the harm each one can do
pages.c07-p03: Describe social engineering techniques, including phishing, smishing, vishing, pretexting and shoulder surfing
pages.c07-p04: Spot the warning signs of a phishing message and know what to do if you receive one
pages.c07-p05: Explain what makes a password strong and how passphrases and password managers help
pages.c07-p06: Explain how two-factor and multi-factor authentication protect accounts
pages.c07-p07: Explain what encryption is, use a Caesar cipher, and explain why the HTTPS padlock matters
pages.c07-p08: Describe how firewalls, anti-malware, updates and backups protect computer systems

q.q: Which is the best description of cyber security?
o: Making computers and networks run as quickly as possible
Building websites and apps that are easy for people to use
Repairing broken hardware such as printers and keyboards
Protecting systems, networks, accounts and data from attack or damage
q.why: Cyber security is all about protection.

q.q: In the CIA triad, which word does the letter I stand for?
q.why: Integrity means the data is correct and has not been changed without permission.

q.q: Someone reads a teacher's private emails but changes nothing. Which part of the CIA triad has been broken?
q.why: Someone has seen data they should not see.

q.q: Pupils cannot reach the school website for a whole day because of an attack. Which part of the CIA triad is affected?
q.why: Availability means systems work when people need them.

q.q: A pupil secretly changes their exam mark on the school system. Which part of the triad is broken?
q.why: The data is no longer correct.

q.q: Why can attacking a hospital's systems do as much harm as stealing its data?
o: If the computers stop working, operations can be cancelled
Hospital data is never worth anything to criminals
Hospitals do not store any personal data
q.why: Systems are valuable too.

q.q: Which of these threats to data is NOT caused by a criminal?
o: A worm spreading across a network
A phishing email stealing a password
A spilled drink destroying a laptop
q.why: Accidents like spills, fires and power cuts can destroy data too.

q.q: 'Only your teachers and parents can see your report' is an example of...
q.why: Only the right people can see the data.

q.q: What does malware mean?
o: Software that contains a few small bugs
Software written on purpose to cause harm
Hardware that has broken down and stopped working
Software that has not been updated for years
q.why: Malware is short for malicious software.

q.q: Which malware spreads across a network by itself, without anyone opening a file?
q.why: A worm is standalone and spreads by itself.

q.q: A free 'Robux generator' app secretly lets someone control your laptop. What type of malware is it?
q.why: It is disguised as something you want.

q.q: A hospital's files are suddenly scrambled and a message demands cryptocurrency. What kind of malware is doing this?
q.why: It holds your files to ransom.

q.q: Malware that secretly records every key you press is called a keylogger. Which type of malware is it?
q.why: It secretly records your key presses.

q.q: How does a virus differ from a worm?
o: A virus needs a person to open or share an infected file
A virus is a standalone program
A virus spreads by itself across a network
A virus spreads to thousands of computers in minutes
q.why: A virus attaches to files and needs people to spread it; a worm spreads alone.

q.q: Which malware floods you with unwanted adverts and pop-ups?
q.why: Adware is often bundled with free software.

q.q: What can a trojan do once installed?
o: Encrypt every file and demand payment straight away
Fix security holes in the operating system for you
Spread by itself to thousands of computers in minutes
Open a 'back door' so an attacker can control the computer
q.why: Trojans pretend to be useful but let attackers in.

q.q: Your browser home page changes by itself and pop-ups appear with no browser open. What do these suggest?
o: The Wi-Fi signal is too weak
The device may be infected with malware
q.why: These are warning signs of infection.

q.q: A ransom note appears on a school computer. What should you do?
o: Pay the ransom quickly so the files come back
Don't click anything and tell your teacher straight away
Click the note to find out how to unlock the files
Restart the computer and carry on with your work
q.why: Technicians can isolate the machine.

q.q: What stops most malware from getting in?
o: Keeping the computer in a cool room
Thinking before you click, open or install
q.why: Most malware needs you to let it in.

q.q: What is social engineering?
o: Tricking or manipulating people into giving away information or access
Using powerful software to guess passwords very quickly
Scrambling data so that only the right person can read it
Spreading malware across a network by itself
q.why: It attacks the human, often called the weakest link.

q.q: A text message claims to be from a delivery company and asks you to pay a redelivery fee. This is...
q.why: SMS + phishing = smishing.

q.q: Which of these is an example of shoulder surfing?
o: Sending fake emails to many people
Browsing the web on a tablet
Watching someone type their password or PIN
q.why: It is simply looking over someone's shoulder.

q.q: Someone rings pretending to be a parent and makes up a story to get a pupil's login. This is...
q.why: A pretext is an invented story.

q.q: Why do social engineering attacks often work even when the computer is well protected?
o: It uses very expensive hacking equipment
It does not need any internet connection
It plays on human feelings like fear and trust
It only works on old, out-of-date computers
q.why: It targets people, who can be rushed or tricked.

q.q: A caller says they are from your bank's fraud team and asks for the code just sent to your phone. This is...
q.why: Vishing is phishing by voice call.

q.q: 'See who viewed your profile!' is a phishing message playing on which feeling?
q.why: Curiosity tempts you to click.

q.q: 'This is IT support, we need your password to fix your account' plays on which feeling?
q.why: Pretending to be someone in authority uses trust.

q.q: Which is a good way to beat shoulder surfing?
o: Type your password in as quickly as you possibly can
Turn the screen brightness up so it is easier to see
Use the same password on every account you have
Lock your screen with Windows key + L when you walk away
q.why: Also shield the keyboard and never type while watched.

q.q: What is spear phishing?
o: Phishing aimed at one specific person using details found online
Phishing that hides a worm inside an email attachment
Phishing carried out through a voice phone call
Phishing sent by text message to thousands of people
q.why: It is targeted, so it is more convincing.

q.q: Which is the most reliable sign that an email is phishing?
o: It was sent early in the morning before school
It is only a few lines long and has no pictures
It asks you to type your password into a linked page
It has the company's logo at the top of it
q.why: Genuine companies never ask for your password via a link.

q.q: How can you check where a link in an email really goes, without clicking it?
o: Hover over it, or press and hold, to see the real address
Click it quickly and then close the page
Forward it to friends to see if it works
Reply to the sender and ask where it goes
q.why: Hovering reveals the true web address.

q.q: In https://login.steam.com.free-skins.net/offer, what is the real website?
q.why: The real domain is the part just before the first single slash.

q.q: Which number can you forward a scam text message to in the UK?
q.why: 7726 spells SPAM on an old keypad.

q.q: Where can you forward a scam email in the UK?
q.why: The NCSC takes scam emails at report@phishing.gov.uk.

q.q: An email starts 'Dear Customer' instead of your name. Which warning sign is this?
q.why: Genuine messages usually use your name.

q.q: An email says 'Act within 24 hours or your account will be deleted!' Which warning sign is this?
q.why: Pressure to act now is a red flag.

q.q: The display name says PayPal but the address is paypa1-alerts@mail-secure.xyz. What does this suggest?
o: The message is definitely from PayPal
q.why: Check the real sender address, not just the display name.

q.q: You think a 'payment failed' email might be real. What is the safest thing to do?
o: Click the link in the email and log in quickly
Forward the email to a friend to check
Open the app or type the address yourself and log in there
Reply to the email with your card details
q.why: Don't use the link in the message.

q.q: In https://www.bbc.co.uk/news, what is the most important part for checking the real website?
q.why: It is the bit just before the first single forward slash.

q.q: You clicked a phishing link and typed your password. What should you do?
o: Keep quiet about it, because it is embarrassing
Tell an adult immediately so the password can be changed
Delete the email and try to forget all about it
Wait a week or two to see if anything happens
q.why: The faster it is changed, the less damage is done.

q.q: Which of these passwords would be hardest for software to crack?
q.why: It is the longest and made of random words.

q.q: Which describes a brute force attack on a password?
o: A virus that deletes files from a hard drive
Physically smashing a computer to get at the data
Tricking someone into telling you their password
Software trying every possible password until one works
q.why: It tries combinations very quickly, billions a second.

q.q: Why is reusing one password on lots of websites risky?
o: If one site is hacked, your other accounts stay safe
It makes logging in to each site faster
Websites charge you for reused passwords
It is against the law to reuse passwords
q.why: Criminals try stolen passwords on other sites.

q.q: What does a password manager do?
o: Creates and stores strong passwords, unlocked by one master password
Deletes any accounts that you have not used for a long time
Encrypts every file that is stored on your hard drive
Blocks viruses and worms from ever reaching your computer
q.why: You only remember the master password.

q.q: What matters most for making a password hard to crack?
q.why: Each extra character multiplies the number of possible passwords.

q.q: What does the National Cyber Security Centre recommend for a strong password?
q.why: e.g. CactusTrumpetHarbour.

q.q: Why is P@ssw0rd a weak password?
o: It only uses lower-case letters and no numbers
It is far too long for most people to remember
It does not contain any letters, only symbols
Swapping letters for symbols is a trick the software already knows
q.why: Cracking software tries these swaps.

q.q: Why is Patrick2012 a weak password?
o: It starts with a capital letter, which is banned
It is too long for most websites to accept
It contains a number, which makes it easier to guess
A name and birth year can be found on social media
q.why: Personal details are easy to find and guess.

q.q: Which password is the most important to protect, because it can reset the others?
q.why: Email can be used to reset every other password.

q.q: Why should you never share your password, even with a best friend?
o: Anything done from your account will look like it was done by you
Your friend's computer may not accept the password
Sharing a password slows down your account for everyone
Passwords stop working as soon as they have been shared
q.why: Friendships change, and you are responsible for your account.

q.q: What does authentication mean?
o: Scrambling data so no one can read it
Making a backup copy of your files
Proving you are who you say you are
Blocking traffic using a set of rules
q.why: The system checks your details before letting you in.

q.q: Which login uses two different types of factor?
o: Password and a code from an authenticator app
Two different passwords for one account
A password and a four-digit PIN
q.why: Something you know + something you have.

q.q: Unlocking a phone with your fingerprint uses which type of factor?
q.why: Biometrics are 'something you are'.

q.q: A stranger messages: 'Oops, I sent my login code to your number, please send it back.' What should you do?
o: Send it to them, because that is the helpful thing to do
Never share it: they are trying to get into your account
Post the code online so that they are able to find it
Reply asking who they are first, and then send it
q.why: This is a classic account takeover scam.

q.q: What is MFA short for?
q.why: Two or more factors.

q.q: A security key or bank card is an example of...
q.why: It is an object only you should have.

q.q: Which second factor is the weakest option?
q.why: Texts can sometimes be redirected.

q.q: How often does an authenticator app usually show a new code?
q.why: It shows a new 6-digit code every 30 seconds.

q.q: Your phone asks you to approve a sign-in you did not start. What should you do?
o: Tap No and change your password
Ignore it and keep the same password
Tap Yes and then log out
Tap Yes to stop the messages
q.why: Someone else knows your password.

q.q: Why is a password and a PIN not true two-factor authentication?
o: A PIN is too short to count
q.why: 2FA needs two different types of factor.

q.q: What is encryption?
o: Scrambling data so only someone with the key can read it
Copying data to another device as a backup
Proving that you are who you say you are
Checking network traffic against a set of rules
q.why: Even if intercepted, encrypted data cannot be read.

q.q: Using a Caesar cipher with a key of 3, what does CAT become?
q.why: Each letter moves 3 places along: C→F, A→D, T→W.

q.q: Using a Caesar cipher with a key of 3, what does HELLO become?
q.why: Each letter moves 3 places: H→K, E→H, L→O, O→R.

q.q: The ciphertext KHOOR was made with a Caesar key of 3. What is the plaintext?
q.why: Decrypt by shifting each letter back 3 places.

q.q: Using a Caesar cipher with a key of 3, what does the letter Y become?
q.why: Y→Z→A→B: the alphabet wraps round.

q.q: After a message has been encrypted, what is the scrambled version called?
q.why: Ciphertext is what an interceptor would see.

q.q: In a Caesar cipher, what is the key?
o: The total number of letters in the message
The number of places each letter is shifted
The first letter of the message
The name of the person receiving it
q.why: e.g. shift by 3.

q.q: Why is the Caesar cipher easy to crack?
o: It needs an internet connection to work
It only works for messages in Latin
It can only be used on numbers
There are only 25 possible keys to try
q.why: You can try every shift quickly.

q.q: A website shows a padlock and its address starts https://. What does this prove?
o: The connection between you and the site is encrypted
The website has no adverts or pop-ups
The website is definitely genuine and honest
The website is run by the government
q.why: It shows HTTPS encryption, not honesty.

q.q: Why should you not log in to a site using HTTP on public Wi-Fi?
o: HTTP sites are not able to show login boxes
Data is sent as plaintext, so others could read it
HTTP is much slower than an old dial-up connection
HTTP sites always contain hidden malware
q.why: HTTPS encrypts; HTTP does not.

q.q: What is the job of a firewall?
o: Makes the passwords on your accounts stronger
Cools down the processor when it gets hot
Checks and filters network traffic using rules
Creates backup copies of all your files
q.why: It controls what data can come in and go out.

q.q: Why should you install software updates promptly?
o: They delete old files to free up space
They often patch security holes attackers could use
They change the colours of the screen
They are required by law every month
q.why: Unpatched holes are how worms like WannaCry spread.

q.q: In the 3-2-1 backup rule, what does the '1' stand for?
q.why: Keeping one copy elsewhere protects against fire, theft and ransomware.

q.q: What happens to a file when anti-malware quarantines it?
o: It is made to run faster
It is emailed to the software company
It is locked away so it cannot run
It is encrypted with a Caesar cipher
q.why: Quarantine isolates the suspicious file.

q.q: What is 'defence in depth'?
o: Using several layers of protection at the same time
Using one very strong firewall and nothing else
Encrypting the same data many times over
q.why: No single defence stops everything.

q.q: Which of these can a firewall NOT stop?
o: Data that breaks its rules coming in
You typing your password into a phishing site
q.why: A firewall cannot stop your own choices.

q.q: In the 3-2-1 backup rule, what does the '2' stand for?
q.why: e.g. laptop and external drive.

q.q: How does anti-malware software recognise known malware?
o: It compares files against a list of malware signatures
It blocks every file that is downloaded
It checks the size of every file
It asks the user whether each file is safe
q.why: It also watches for suspicious behaviour.

q.q: Why must anti-malware be kept up to date?
o: So it can patch the firewall
So it can recognise new threats
q.why: Out-of-date signatures miss new malware.

q.q: A program suddenly starts encrypting hundreds of files. Why might anti-malware stop it?
o: It is checking for spelling mistakes
It blocks every program that opens files
It is watching for suspicious behaviour
It has a signature for every file you own
q.why: Behaviour like mass encryption suggests ransomware.

q.q: WannaCry only infected computers that had not done what?
o: Made a backup in the last week
Installed a patch released two months earlier
q.why: Prompt updates would have prevented it.

q.q: Which law makes hacking into someone's account illegal?
q.why: Unauthorised access is the first offence under the Computer Misuse Act.

q.q: Under data protection law, which of these counts as personal data?
q.why: It can identify a living person.

q.q: Which UK organisation can fine companies for breaking data protection law?
q.why: The Information Commissioner's Office.

q.q: A club collects members' blood type when it only needs their name and email. Which principle is broken?
q.why: Only collect what you need.

q.q: Why was the Computer Misuse Act passed?
o: People who hacked a BT system could not be properly charged
Ransomware attacks had shut down several hospitals
Far too many people had started buying home computers
The rules on data protection needed to be updated
q.why: No law covered hacking at the time.

q.q: Logging in as a friend using a password you saw them type breaks which offence?
q.why: Getting into an account without permission.

q.q: Flooding a website so it crashes is which Computer Misuse Act offence?
o: Unauthorised acts that impair a computer
q.why: Deliberately stopping a computer from working.

q.q: A company keeps old customers' details for 20 years with no reason. Which principle is broken?
q.why: Don't keep data longer than needed.

q.q: What is a subject access request?
o: Asking for permission to carry out a penetration test
Asking an organisation for a copy of the data it holds about you
Asking the police to investigate a hacker for you
Asking a website to remove all of its adverts
q.why: It is one of your rights over your data.

q.q: A pupil says 'I was only messing about' after using a friend's login. Is that a defence?
o: Yes, jokes are not covered by the law
No, it can still break the Computer Misuse Act
Yes, if the friend told them the password once
No, but only adults can break the law
q.why: Unauthorised access is illegal even as a joke.

q.q: What is the main difference between an ethical hacker and a criminal hacker?
o: Criminal hackers only ever work at night
Ethical hackers use more powerful computers
Ethical hackers have permission from the system owner
Ethical hackers never find any weaknesses
q.why: Permission makes it legal.

q.q: What is penetration testing?
o: Testing how strong and scratch-proof a phone screen is
A type of malware that gets into networks through holes
Installing a firewall on every computer in a network
An agreed, planned attack on a system to find weaknesses
q.why: It is followed by a report to fix the weaknesses.

q.q: CyberFirst competitions and courses are run by which organisation?
q.why: The NCSC is part of GCHQ.

q.q: A pupil discovers a way to see other pupils' files on the school network. What should they do?
o: Look at a few files to check it works
Report it privately to a teacher without testing it
Tell everyone in the class about it
Post about it online as a warning
q.why: Reporting responsibly, without accessing data, is right.

q.q: What happens to what an ethical hacker finds?
o: It is reported privately to the owner so it can be fixed
It is used to steal money from the system's owner
It is posted publicly online to warn everyone at once
It is sold to whoever offers the most money online
q.why: Criminal hackers use or sell what they find.

q.q: What is a bug bounty programme?
o: A course that teaches pupils how to debug code
Rewards paid to people who report security flaws responsibly
A competition to write the most bugs in a program
A fine for companies whose software has bugs
q.why: Some companies pay for responsible reports.

q.q: Which cyber security job examines computers and phones after a crime to find evidence?
q.why: They often work with the police.

q.q: What are Capture the Flag (CTF) competitions?
o: Safe, legal puzzles such as cracking a cipher
Games played on a sports field
Contests to hack real school networks
q.why: Practise only on legal training sites and competitions.

q.q: Why are cyber security skills in high demand?
o: Only government jobs need these skills
There are not enough trained people to fill the jobs
Cyber security work needs no training
Most cyber security jobs are being removed
q.why: Northern Ireland, especially Belfast, has a growing cyber industry.
